Deceivings
dee-SEE-vingz
n. plural (acts or instances of deception; fraudulent indulgences practiced openly)
Old French decevoir, from Latin decipere, to catch or ensnare — instances of leading others, or oneself, into false belief.

Biblical Definition

And shall receive the reward of unrighteousness, as they that count it pleasure to riot in the day time. Spots they are and blemishes, sporting themselves with their own deceivings while they feast with you.

Peter's description of false teachers reaches a particularly unsettling detail: these are not secretive sinners hiding their corruption, but men who riot in the day time, feasting openly at the church's own love feasts while sporting themselves with their own deceivings. The phrase pictures self-indulgent delusion as a kind of game these men play with themselves, taking pleasure not only in sin but in the deceptions that excuse it, and doing so in full public view, embedded within the fellowship of believers rather than lurking outside it. Deceivings here names a corruption so brazen it has stopped bothering to hide, the mark of a conscience Peter describes elsewhere in the same letter as having eyes full of adultery, that cannot cease from sin.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), from DECEIVE: instances of deception; fraudulent delusions indulged in and enjoyed by the deceiver.

expand to see more

DECEIVE, v.t. To mislead; to cause to believe what is false.

DECEIVINGS, n. plural. Instances or acts of deception, here self-indulged.

Describes false teachers sporting themselves with their own delusions.

Practiced openly, at the church's own feasts, not in secret.

Marks a conscience so corrupted it no longer hides its sin.

Key Scripture

2Pe 2:13 — "And shall receive the reward of unrighteousness, as they that count it pleasure to riot in the day time. Spots they are and blemishes, sporting themselves with their own deceivings while they feast with you;"

Modern Corruption

A church culture that assumes false teachers must be secretive or obviously hypocritical can be caught off guard by Peter's description: men sporting themselves with their own deceivings openly, at the fellowship's own table, unashamed rather than hidden.

expand to see more

It is comforting to assume corruption in the church will announce itself through obvious secrecy or visible shame. Peter describes the opposite: brazen, daytime indulgence, feasting openly with the very believers being deceived.

The corrective is vigilance that does not rely on a false teacher's discomfort as a warning sign; Peter's spots and blemishes language calls the church to discern by doctrine and fruit, not merely by the presence or absence of apparent shame, since the men he describes have none left.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek apatais, deceits or delusions, from apatao, to deceive, cheat — here used reflexively of men entertaining themselves with their own delusions rather than merely deceiving others.

expand to see more

Deceivings names self-indulged, brazen delusion, not hidden deception.

Peter describes false teachers feasting openly at the church's own table.

The corruption is practiced without shame, in full public view.

Discernment by doctrine and fruit is required, not reliance on visible guilt.

This marks a conscience Peter elsewhere calls unable to cease from sin.

Usage

"Sporting themselves with their own deceivings while they feast with you."

"Brazen, daytime indulgence rather than hidden corruption."

"A call to discern false teaching by doctrine, not by apparent shame."
